paras: The whipping of Kate Brown was an assault on a Black woman at Hillsboro, Caroline County, Maryland, on August 3, 1885, when two white men dragged her from a magistrate's office and whipped her. She had been waiting there for their trial on a charge of beating her in her own house a few days earlier. The only known account, a Baltimore letter in the New York Freeman, presented the case as one of several outrages against Black Marylanders that the white press ignored.

According to the Freeman's correspondent, the two men had "inhumanly beaten" Brown in her own house a few days before the attack. The men were brought before the local "Squire" for trial, and Brown was at his office awaiting the hearing.

On the 3rd, the two men seized Brown at the Squire's office, dragged her out and whipped her a second time. The correspondent wrote that "the second whipping was more severe than the first." Several bystanders gave her no help, and the constable, by this account, "slyly slipped away to Cape May."

The Freeman's headline announced "No Arrests," though the same letter later said that "the Eastern Shore brutes are held under slight bail for appearance to court," which appears to refer to Brown's attackers. No report of a trial or its outcome was found.

The New York Freeman, a Black weekly, ran the story on August 15 in a Baltimore letter dated August 10 under the headlines "BRUTALITY IN MARYLAND. WHAT ARE YOU GOING TO DO ABOUT IT?" and "A Colored Woman Taken from the Court Room and Brutally Beaten." The correspondent called the attackers "cowardly white brutes" and paired the case with the assault of a 17-year-old Black girl at Hampstead by a white man who had not been arrested. He charged that the papers had been "so quiet about these outrages that one would think nothing had happened," although they had editorialized at once against Cooper, whose lynching the letter also mentioned, over his alleged assault on a white girl. No white newspaper account of the attack was found.
